requirements.requirement: Restore the supplied tickets.sql export into a PostgreSQL database named helpdesk while retaining the imported ticket IDs and text.
requirements.summary: The export created the tickets table and imported all three rows. Direct queries before and after restart show exactly IDs 1, 2, and 100 with subjects Printer queue, Scanner cable, and Office move.

requirements.requirement: Repair automatic ID allocation so inserts without an explicit ID receive unique IDs greater than the imported maximum.
requirements.summary: The sequence was set to the imported maximum of 100. Transactional tests allocated 102 before restart and 103 afterward, both greater than 100; the test rows were rolled back and the imported rows remained unchanged.
tickets.sql remains at the required path with SHA-256 5a9b51de0c539f9ffedd0ca1424be6549bbef62a5414b6545d879d9c1be973c5, matching the preparation baseline.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel, using software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: RHEL 9.8 and kernel 5.14.0-687.20.1.el9_8.x86_64 match the pre-executor platform and remained unchanged after execution. PostgreSQL 13.23 was installed from the RHEL 9 AppStream repository, and final package health was clean.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct evidence. The helpdesk database contains the original tickets, default ID allocation works above the imported maximum, the source export is unchanged, and the RHEL release and kernel were preserved. The provider-wide restart protocol also fully demonstrates node1 recovery and persistence.
limitations: Requirement preserve-source-export cited unknown evidence IDs: seeded-state-node1

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Package installation, database initialization and enablement, database restoration, and sequence repair directly served the task. Transactional insert tests were bounded evidence collection; their rows were reverted, while normal nontransactional sequence advancement remained and did not impair the required allocation behavior. The reboot served the mandatory restart protocol. No failed services, damaged package state, unsafe PostgreSQL exposure, or abandoned transient reboot units are evident; PostgreSQL listens only on loopback. The restart protocol is complete: a healthy pre-restart boot, acknowledged reboot, changed boot identity, and recovered service, source file, database rows, allocation behavior, OS, and kernel were directly observed and independently corroborated by lifecycle boot snapshots.
